# Appendix B — Gate and Review Checklists {.unnumbered}

The checklists in this appendix turn the book's gates into observable questions. They are review aids, not a substitute for judgment: a checked box records that someone asked the question, not that the answer was good.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="When to Use This Chapter"}
- A brief, outline, pilot, chapter or release is approaching a gate.
- A reviewer needs a consistent set of questions for a change.
- A team is adapting the gate process to its own risk profile.
- A previous review missed a required check and needs a corrective checklist.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false title="Key Takeaway"}
A checklist is useful when every item can fail and the failure changes the decision. Keep the list short enough to run and specific enough to produce evidence.
:::

## B.1 The Gate and Review Checklist Library

**Definition.** A gate checklist is an ordered set of questions that a reviewer answers with evidence before an owner decides whether work may pass a gate. A review checklist applies the same idea to one change; it is not a scorecard of the author's effort.

**Purpose.** The checklist makes a gate repeatable across reviewers and authors. It also makes omissions visible: if a check cannot be answered, the work is not ready, even when the prose looks finished. The owner can then decide whether to fix the gap, approve an explicit exception or delay the gate.

**What it includes.** The brief gate checks reader, promise, non-goals, evidence, owner and change trigger. The outline gate checks exit evidence, dependencies, pilot choice and profile coverage. The pilot gate checks approved preconditions, section scope, source discipline and conformance evidence. The chapter review checks the chapter and section elements, examples, sources, cross-references and exact commit. The release gate checks the approved commit, seven assets, manifest, checksums, format inspection, licensing and immutable release/catalog behavior.

For each item, record the reviewed commit, checker, result and supporting evidence. A checked item without evidence is unresolved. The owner records the gate decision after review.

**Brief gate**
- [ ] Are the reader, observable promise, scope and non-goals explicit?
- [ ] Are the evidence method, accountable owner and change/review trigger recorded?

**Outline gate**
- [ ] Does each chapter have a distinct outcome and exit evidence, with dependencies identified?
- [ ] Are profile coverage, the pilot section and its exact file path recorded?

**Pilot gate**
- [ ] Are the brief and outline approved, and is the submitted text limited to the approved pilot scope?
- [ ] Has an independent reviewer checked the exact commit, examples, sources, profile conformance and recorded exceptions, with blocking findings resolved?

**Chapter review**
Use the Review Checklist in B.2 and attach its evidence to the reviewed commit.

**Release gate**
- [ ] Are the complete manuscript, licensing, attribution and exact source commit approved?
- [ ] Are the toolkit/profile pins and recorded build environment consistent with the proposal?
- [ ] Do all seven files exist: HTML ZIP, PDF, DOCX, Markdown edition, source ZIP, manifest and checksums?
- [ ] Do identity, checksum membership, hashes, format checks and human layout inspection pass?
- [ ] Is the owner's publication authorization recorded, with the immutable tag and catalog/withdrawal plan identified?

**Why it is needed.** Reviews drift when they depend on memory. One reviewer checks sources; another checks structure; a third focuses on wording. The author cannot tell which omissions were deliberate. A shared checklist gives the gate a floor and makes the review record comparable across changes.

**Example.** *Illustrative only: a chapter review.* The reviewer opens the checklist, marks the chapter's reader outcome, the four unit labels, the closing elements, the Worked Example and Further Reading, the source ledger entries and the exact commit. Two items cannot be answered: a normative claim cites a secondary summary that does not establish the stated requirement, and a cross-reference target is missing. The verdict is changes requested because the claim lacks adequate support and the reference cannot be followed.


::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon=false title="Common Pitfall"}
A checked box is not evidence. If the checklist cannot name the source, command or artifact that supports the answer, the review is recording agreement rather than verification.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false title="Decision & Trade-off"}
Checklists can be short and generic or long and risk-specific.

| Checklist style | Choose when | Consequences |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Short universal list | Routine chapters and small changes | Fast; may miss domain-specific evidence. |
| Gate-specific list | Brief, outline, pilot, release or licensing decisions | Stronger evidence; more review time. |
| Risk-triggered additions | Security, regulated data or high-impact publication | Targeted coverage; requires a clear trigger. |

Start with the shortest list that catches the failure modes you have seen. Add an item only when its absence has caused or could cause a real defect.
:::

## B.2 Worked Example — Running a Chapter Checklist

*In practice:* a reviewer runs the chapter checklist before reading for style.

1. Record the exact reviewed commit and the applicable profile.
2. Check When to Use This Chapter and Key Takeaway before the first section.
3. Check each content section for Definition, Purpose, What it includes and Why it is needed.
4. Check Example, Common Pitfall and Decision & Trade-off in order.
5. Check Worked Example, Review Checklist and Further Reading placement.
6. Check labels, references and local images against the reading order.
7. Check source claims against the source ledger.
8. Record unresolved items and classify them by consequence.
9. Post the verdict and the exact commands actually run.

In the illustrative review, the chapter passes structure but fails one source check and one reference check. The reviewer does not rewrite the chapter; they report the locations and the evidence needed. The author fixes both and the reviewer re-runs on the new commit.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Review Checklist"}
- Is the reviewed commit recorded and still the exact HEAD?
- Are the chapter-level elements present and ordered?
- Are every content section's four unit elements and three closure elements present?
- Does the Worked Example end with a Review Checklist?
- Is Further Reading the last numbered section?
- Do references and local assets resolve?
- Are sources real, checkable and adequate for the claim?
- Is every finding classified and every blocking finding owned?
:::
